title: Animals' rights
hook: don't overload, don't brand faces, don't make them targets (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, 'aqd, the contract, and your line: clear terms. Clear words, a free yes, and no gamble hidden inside. Did you read something before you agreed to it? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

Tears, running from a camel's eyes. That's where a report in Abu Dawud begins, in a walled garden in Medina belonging to a man of the Ansar. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ steps inside, and the camel tied there sees him and begins to groan. He goes over and strokes it behind the ears until it settles. Then he asks: whose camel is this? A young man comes running. And the Prophet tells him to fear God about this animal, because it has complained to him that its owner starves it and wears it out. Yesterday, contracts between people who can speak for themselves. Today, the ones who can't.
screen: `A CAMEL IN A WALLED GARDEN.` → `IT GROANS, THEN SETTLES.` → `IT COMPLAINED OF YOU.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an sets the frame. In surah six, it says that every creature on the earth and every bird that flies on two wings are communities like you, and that they too will be gathered to their Lord. Communities with their own lives, not furniture. From that frame the fiqh books draw duties, and today's three come straight from the hadith. First, don't overload. Another report in Abu Dawud tells of the Prophet passing a camel so thin its back had nearly reached its belly, and saying: fear God about these animals that cannot speak; ride them while they are fit, and eat of them while they are fit. The jurists turned that into a rule: an owner must feed an animal and may not work it beyond its strength. Second, don't brand or strike faces. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet forbids hitting the face and branding the face, and when he passes a donkey branded on its face, he curses whoever did it. The face, it seems, is protected even on a donkey. Third, don't make them targets. Also in Sahih Muslim, Ibn Umar comes across young men who have tied up a bird and are shooting at it. They scatter when they see him, and he tells them the Prophet cursed anyone who makes a living thing a target. So the fiqh books speak of an animal's rights the way they speak of a neighbor's: food, rest, a fair load, a face left unbranded. A camel cannot file a complaint. The tradition says it filed one anyway, and the Prophet heard it.
screen: `COMMUNITIES LIKE YOU.` · `DON'T OVERLOAD: FEED AND REST THEM.` · `DON'T BRAND OR STRIKE THE FACE.` · `DON'T MAKE THEM TARGETS.`

segments.voice: Care for an animal, even from here. If there's a pet near you, go to it now, check its water, and just sit with it for the length of the bell. If there isn't, bring to mind an animal you see often: a neighbor's dog, a bird on the wire, a horse on a farm you pass. What does it need that only a person can give it? Food, water, shade, a lighter load? Hold it in mind kindly. If you pray, you can remember it there. The bell holds the time.
Animals' rights. In Islamic law, what an animal is owed: food, rest, a fair load, a face left unharmed, and never to be used as a target. Today's word.

Your line: they have rights. Today, put out water, slow down for a bird, or take a look at what a working animal is carrying. Tomorrow, how old law meets new medicine. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Islamic law requires owners to feed and rest their animals and not to overwork them, and forbids striking or branding their faces and using living creatures as targets.

notes: 6:38 paraphrased (Pickthall: 'peoples like unto you'); 'gathered to their Lord' paraphrases the end of the verse. Confirm.
Abu Dawud 2549: confirm details (tears, stroking behind the ears, the young Ansari owner, 'starves it and wears it out').
Abu Dawud 2548: confirm wording paraphrase and number (Sahl ibn al-Hanzaliyyah).
Muslim 2116–2117 and 1958: confirm numbers; some versions say a hen rather than a bird.
Jurists' rules on feeding and not overworking: confirm general framing (some schools allow a judge to compel an owner).
'The face, it seems, is protected even on a donkey' is the narrator's observation.

Editor: fixed Abu Dawud 2548 paraphrase (the report says ride them and eat them while fit, not 'leave them'); Ibn Umar scene matched to Muslim 1958 (the young men scatter when they see him); 'many of them' cut; hook opening and close varied from the range's repeated scene-fragment openers.
